rows.name: fifo-why
rows.question: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does index equality alone not distinguish full from empty? Give the two concrete capacity-17 states and show how your actual implementation distinguishes them.
rows.answer:
Index equality alone is ambiguous because advancing an index by 17 brings it back to the same position modulo 17. In this implementation, the insertion index is computed as `(head_ + count_) % capacity`; it is not stored separately.

The two concrete states are:
- Empty initially: `head_ = 0`, `count_ = 0`, so the insertion index is `(0 + 0) % 17 = 0`, equal to the head. `pop` returns false because `count_ == 0`.
- Full after pushing values 0 through 16: `head_ = 0`, `count_ = 17`, so the insertion index is `(0 + 17) % 17 = 0`, also equal to the head. `push` returns false because `count_ == capacity`, before modifying any data.

Thus, both states have equal head and insertion indices, but the explicit count distinguishes empty from full while allowing all 17 slots to be used.
rows.usefulPrefix: Index equality alone is ambiguous because advancing an index by 17 brings it back to the same position modulo 17.
rows.note: Exact earlier implementation stores no separate tail: initialhead0/count0/insertion0 versusfullhead0/count17/insertion0. Count distinguishes actual states, fullrejectbeforewrite correct.

rows.name: floating-counterexample
rows.question: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Under IEEE binary32, round after each addition and forbid reassociation. Evaluate (16777216 + -16777216) + 1 and 16777216 + (-16777216 + 1). Then change the leftmost operand to positive 16777216, the middle operand to 1, and the last operand to -16777216. Compare both parenthesizations of that changed triple. Explain representability at each intermediate step; do not simply cite nonassociativity.
rows.answer:
With IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, both original expressions evaluate to 1. For the changed triple, the left-parenthesized expression evaluates to 0, while the right-parenthesized expression evaluates to 1.

Binary32 has 24 bits of significand precision. All integers from −16777216 through 16777216 are exactly representable; just above positive 16777216, adjacent representable values are spaced 2 apart.

Original triple:
• (16777216 + −16777216) + 1: the first addition gives exactly 0, and the second gives exactly 1.
• 16777216 + (−16777216 + 1): the inner addition gives −16777215, which is exactly representable. Adding 16777216 then gives exactly 1. Neither intermediate requires rounding away any information.

Changed triple:
• (16777216 + 1) + −16777216: the first exact mathematical sum is 16777217, which is not representable. It lies halfway between 16777216 and 16777218; ties-to-even selects 16777216, whose significand has an even low bit. The second addition therefore cancels exactly to 0.
• 16777216 + (1 + −16777216): the inner sum is −16777215, which is exactly representable because the spacing on that side of the negative boundary is 1. The outer addition then gives exactly 1.

Thus the original triple does not demonstrate different results, but the changed triple does: only its left parenthesization loses the added 1 during intermediate rounding.
rows.usefulPrefix: With IEEE binary32’s default round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, both original expressions evaluate to 1.
rows.note: Explicit RNE assumption. Original triple both1 with representable-16777215, changedleft16777217tie rounds16777216 then0; right-16777215+16777216=1. Loweven significand and spacing2above/1below boundary correct. No claim other rounding modes give same result.

rows.name: quorum-counterexample
rows.question: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Five replicas A,B,C,D,E retain the highest version. A writer finishes after three acknowledgements. A reader queries any three and returns the highest version, without write-back. Prove or disprove linearizability including reads overlapping an incomplete write: give a fully ordered execution with two nonoverlapping reads and show the attempted linearization contradiction. Then change only the reader to write the selected version to three replicas before returning and explain whether this fixes the counterexample.
rows.answer:
Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a read can expose an incomplete write, and a later, nonoverlapping read can return the older value. Writing the selected version back to three replicas before returning fixes this counterexample, assuming replicas acknowledge only after retaining that version or a higher one.

Here is a fully ordered execution. Initially, all five replicas hold version 0, with value x:
1. A writer invokes W, writing version 1 with value y. Only A receives it and acknowledges. The state is A=1, B=C=D=E=0. W remains incomplete because it has only one acknowledgement.
2. Reader R1 is invoked and queries A, B, C. Their replies are 1, 0, 0. R1 returns y and completes; no replicas are changed.
3. Only after R1 completes, reader R2 is invoked and queries B, D, E. All three reply with version 0. R2 returns x and completes.
4. After R2 completes, W reaches B and C and obtains its remaining acknowledgements. W returns successfully. The final state is A=B=C=1, D=E=0.

The attempted linearization is impossible. R1 returning y requires W to precede R1 in the sequential register history, since W is the only write of y. Real-time order requires R1 to precede R2. Thus W must precede R1, which must precede R2—but R2 returns x even though there is no intervening write restoring x. Although W overlaps both reads and could ordinarily be placed anywhere within that interval, no placement satisfies both results.

Now change only the reader to write back its selected version and wait for three acknowledgements before returning. In this execution, R1 selects version 1 and can write it to A, B, C. When R1 returns, those three replicas retain version 1 or higher. R2’s query set B, D, E includes B, so R2 cannot return version 0. More generally, any two sets of three among five replicas intersect: 3 + 3 > 5. Because versions never decrease, every read begun after R1 completes encounters at least one replica holding R1’s selected version or higher.

This also handles an incomplete write: a read may select its version, but before exposing it to the caller, the read makes that version quorum-visible. The incomplete write can then be included in the linearized history before that read, and subsequent reads cannot go backward. Together with the same intersection argument for completed writes, this gives the standard linearizable quorum-register construction, provided versions uniquely order writes consistently with real-time write order—for example, with a single writer using increasing versions. If multiple writers merely invent versions without ensuring that property, read write-back alone does not establish linearizability.
rows.usefulPrefix: Without read write-back, the protocol is not linearizable: a read can expose an incomplete write, and a later, nonoverlapping read can return the older value.
rows.note: Fully ordered W1onlyA, R1ABC1 completes, R2BDE0, thenW completesB/C: W<R1<R2 forced butR2old impossible. Readwriteback3intersects every later3 and monotonicversions prevent regression. Singlewriterincreasing or uniqueRTcompatibletags explicitly required for general claim; not silentMWprotocolassumption.

rows.name: quorum-why
rows.question: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why does the second read have to respect a value returned by the first read even if the writer never completed? State the relevant real-time order and distinguish it from requiring every unfinished operation to complete.
rows.answer:
Because once the first read returns the new value, any legal linearization must include the pending write and place it before that read—even if the writer never receives enough acknowledgements to return.

For example, initially every replica holds version 0. A pending write of version 1 reaches only A; the first read queries A,B,C and returns 1. After that read returns, the second read is invoked, queries B,C,D, and returns 0. The relevant real-time order is that the first read’s response precedes the second read’s invocation, so the first read must precede the second in the sequential history.

Since the first read returns 1, the write of 1 must precede it in that history. Thus the required order is write 1, first read, second read; with no intervening write, the second read must also return 1, contradicting its return of 0.

This does not require every unfinished operation to complete. Linearizability permits pending operations to be omitted or included by completing them in an extension of the history. Here, omitting this particular write cannot explain the first read’s result, while including it makes the second read’s result illegal. Neither choice produces a valid linearization.
rows.usefulPrefix: Because once the first read returns the new value, any legal linearization must include the pending write and place it before that read—even if the writer never receives enough acknowledgements to return.

rows.name: backend-reconnection
rows.question: Why must desired be recomputed after that failure? Refer to the concrete values in the preceding explanation, and state what is retained across a reconnection.
rows.recognizedQuestion: Why must desired be recomputed after that failure? Refer to the concrete values in the preceding explanation, and state what is retained across a reconnection.
rows.answer:
After B’s failed comparison, `expected` changes from 0 to 1, but the old `desired` remains 1. Retrying those values can successfully compare 1 and store 1, so B returns without incrementing; recomputing `desired = expected + 1` makes the next attempt compare 1 and store 2 instead.

If by “reconnection” you mean the next retry, the same invocation retains its local variables: `expected` holds the value observed by the failed operation, while `desired` stays unchanged unless explicitly recomputed. A spurious failure also requires retrying, with `desired` recomputed from the resulting `expected`. If you mean an actual connection loss and reconnect, this code has no connection or persistence mechanism, so it specifies no state retained across that event.
